doc.title: Duffy Jackson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 17, 1995

title: Sammy Davis Jr., Monty Alexander and preparing for the Basie job
summary: Three years with Sammy Davis Jr., then Monty Alexander for over twenty-two years, and seven months of preparation with fifty Basie tapes before joining.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working with Sinatra: bands, Vegas and the Sands

blocks.x: How about some of the other great vocalists?

Well, after that when I was twenty years old Louie Bellson had a lot to do with getting me to be Sammy Davis Jr.’s drummer, and I was with Sammy for three years off and on at that point. And to back up one of the greatest showmen of all-time, and what was great is that all his arrangements sounded like the Count Basie band and we just had like forty strings included, and as I said before, that too was one of the great jobs to be paid to learn. You know because when you have to back up the great Sammy Davis, but also hold like a sixty piece orchestra together, you better know what you’re doing. And I don’t actually say that I knew what I was doing at all times, but I kept my heart wide open to any positive critique. And everyone had their own opinion of what I was doing, correctly, but Sammy was very gracious to me and I learned a lot from him. And it’s not that we were too close off the stage, because he enjoyed his privacy, and I was told to stay away at certain times, whatever. But the main thing is when we were on the bandstand, he was mine, and I kicked him as hard as I could and he turned around and smiled at me on numerous occasions, you know. But then after that I said well now I’m going to make it in show business, ‘cause I’m with Sammy you know. But then I said hey, I really want to play jazz. I want to get more into being able to express myself away from being an accompanist and more of a show business jazz act, and get into playing with some more straight ahead musicians. And so I started traveling again with Monty Alexander, the great Jamaican pianist. And I played with Monty off and on for over twenty-two years and then all of a sudden I get the call from Count Basie. You know I’d played with Lionel Hampton before that, whatever. And Count was starting to get a little older and Butch Miles, bless his heart, I thought he was never going to leave the band because he was there almost five years. And I said well you know, I hope I get my shot to play. And Butch wanted to give a whole bunch of different drummers an opportunity to play with the band, and plus he wanted to get out on his own and do his own thing too. So the phone rang one night and it was Count himself. And he said, “What are you doing, Duffy?” And I said, “I’m waiting for Butch to get off that band, you know, so I can get there.” But the wild part about it, and this does not happen in any situation that I know of. Count Basie and Butch Miles gave me seven months to prepare. I had seven months knowing that I was going to join the band. So what I did I made around fifty cassette tapes filled with the Count Basie groove from the 30s to the present band. And I studied those tapes every day, every night I fell asleep with the headphones on, you know and woke up playing Basie. And when I joined the band, I did not have to read a note of music.
